title: Protecting Data & Privacy
summary: Handle personal and confidential information the right way, every time.

lessons.title: Know what's sensitive
points: Personal data is anything that identifies a person: names, emails, phone numbers, ID numbers, photos, location.
Some data needs extra care: health, financial, biometric, children's data and passwords.
Follow your organisation's classification labels (for example Public, Internal, Confidential).

lessons.title: Share the minimum
points: Collect and share only what's needed for the task (data minimisation).
Give access to people who need it, and remove access when they no longer do.
Double-check recipients before sending. Autocomplete sends lots of data to the wrong person.
lessons.tip: Ask: does this person need this data, for this purpose, right now?

lessons.title: Store and send it safely
points: Use approved storage and sharing tools, not personal email or personal cloud accounts.
Prefer sharing links with restricted access over attachments, and set expiry dates.
Dispose of paper and devices securely: shredding, and IT-managed wiping.

lessons.title: When something goes wrong
points: Sent data to the wrong person? Lost a file? Report it immediately, even if it seems minor.
Many privacy laws (such as the EU GDPR) have strict deadlines for reporting breaches. GDPR's is 72 hours for organisations to notify the regulator.
Honest, quick reporting is always better than trying to fix it quietly.

questions.q: Which of these is personal data?
questions.why: A phone number can identify a specific person, so it's personal data.

questions.q: Forwarding work files to your personal email so you can work at home is acceptable if you delete them later.
questions.why: Personal accounts are outside your organisation's controls and may break policy or law. Use approved remote-work tools.

options: Collecting and sharing only the data needed for a purpose
questions.why: Holding less data means less to lose, and it's a core principle in privacy laws such as the GDPR.

questions.q: You accidentally emailed a customer list to the wrong external address. What should you do?
options: Report it to your manager/privacy or security team right away
Email again asking them to delete it and tell no one
questions.why: This may be a reportable data breach with legal deadlines. Report it immediately so the right steps are taken.

questions.q: Under the EU GDPR, organisations must generally notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, where feasible.
questions.why: GDPR Article 33 sets the 72-hour expectation (unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms).

questions.q: What's the safest way to share a confidential file with a colleague?
options: Approved sharing tool with access limited to that colleague
Print and leave on their desk
questions.why: Restricted links in approved tools keep access controlled and auditable.

questions.q: Old paper records containing customer details can go in the normal recycling bin.
questions.why: Use secure shredding or confidential waste bins. Discarded paper is a real source of data leaks.

questions.q: A colleague who moved teams still has access to your project's HR folder. What's the right action?
options: Ask the folder owner/IT to remove access they no longer need
Share your password with them too
questions.why: Access should match current need (least privilege). Removing stale access reduces risk.

questions.q: Before sending an email with sensitive data, it's worth double-checking the recipients and attachments.
questions.why: Mis-addressed emails are one of the most common causes of data breaches.

questions.q: Which data usually needs the most protection?
options: Health or financial information about a person
questions.why: Health and financial data can cause serious harm if exposed and often has extra legal protection.
